intro: In 1969, Americans watched two astronauts walk on the Moon. The country was still locked in a Cold War with the Soviet Union. Most homes had one telephone, attached to the wall. Today, people carry more computing power in their pockets than NASA used to reach the Moon. The Soviet Union is gone. The nation looks different too, with more people whose families came from Latin America, Asia and Africa.

This unit covers the years from 1969 to the present. You will read about a scandal that led a president to resign, and about gas lines and rising prices. You will see the Cold War end and a new era of computers and the internet begin. You will also learn about the September 11 attacks, two long wars, a deep recession, a pandemic and several very close elections.

Because this history is recent, people who lived through it often still disagree about what it means. That is normal in a democracy. As you read, look for the facts, notice what supporters and critics argued, and form your own view based on evidence.
bigQuestion: How has the United States changed since 1969, and how have Americans worked through their disagreements about its future?

write.prompt: Choose one change from this unit, such as the end of the Cold War, the internet, the Americans with Disabilities Act or immigration. Explain how it changed life in the United States, using at least two pieces of evidence from the unit.
tips: Start with a clear claim that names the change and its biggest effect.
Use at least two facts, dates or sources from the lessons as evidence.
Explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim.
If people disagreed about the change, describe both sides fairly.
End by connecting the change to life today.

title: America in a Changing World

chapters.title: New American Politics
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Americans' trust in government, and their ideas about its job, change between 1969 and 1990?

story.title: The Night the Wall Opened
story.kicker: On November 9, 1989, a mistake at a press conference opened a wall that had split a city for 28 years.
paragraphs: For 28 years, a concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two. East Germany's Communist government built it in 1961. Its goal was to stop its own people from escaping to West Berlin, which was free and tied to the West. The wall had guard towers, bright lights and armed soldiers. Families were split apart. Many people who tried to cross were caught, and some were killed.

By 1989, change was sweeping across Eastern Europe. The Soviet Union's leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, had said he would not send tanks to keep Communist governments in power. In East Germany, huge crowds marched in the streets. Every week the marches grew. Thousands of East Germans fled to the West through other countries, such as Hungary. The government knew it had to do something.

On the evening of November 9, an East German official named Günter Schabowski held a press conference on live TV. He read a note about new travel rules. A reporter asked when the rules started. Schabowski looked at his papers. He seemed unsure. Then he said that, as far as he knew, they started immediately. In fact, the rules were supposed to begin the next day, with careful controls.

People all over East Berlin heard the news. Thousands rushed to the checkpoints in the wall. At the Bornholmer Street crossing, the crowd grew larger and louder. The guards had no orders. They were badly outnumbered. Late that night, the officer in charge decided to open the gate. People streamed through, laughing and crying. Strangers from West Berlin hugged them and handed out flowers.

Over the next days, people climbed on top of the wall and danced. Some chipped off pieces with hammers to keep. Less than a year later, in October 1990, East and West Germany became one country again. For Americans, who had spent more than 40 years in the Cold War, the open wall was a sign that a long, dangerous era was ending.

The fall of the wall came at the end of two busy decades in the United States. Americans walked on the Moon, argued over a scandal that brought down a president, waited in gas lines and watched prices climb. They also debated what government should and should not do. This chapter tells that story.
story.think: Why do you think a small mistake at a press conference could lead to such a big change? What had to be true already?

lessons.title: Footprints on the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: In July 1969, Apollo 11 astronauts became the first people to walk on the Moon, a high point of the space race.
reading: Richard Nixon became president in January 1969. He was a Republican from California who had been Dwight Eisenhower's vice president. Nixon took over a country divided by the Vietnam War and upset by protests and violence. Just six months later, the nation shared a moment of pride.

On July 20, 1969, the *lunar* module of Apollo 11 landed on the Moon. Astronaut Neil Armstrong climbed down a ladder and stepped onto the dusty ground. Buzz Aldrin soon joined him. Michael Collins circled above in the command ship. About 600 million people around the world watched on television.

The Moon landing was a win in the space race with the Soviet Union. President John F. Kennedy had set the goal in 1961. Thousands of engineers, scientists and workers made it happen. Some were Black women mathematicians, such as Katherine Johnson, who did key calculations at NASA. Over the next few years, 12 American astronauts walked on the Moon. The last *mission* returned in 1972.

words.d: having to do with the Moon
a special trip or job, such as a flight into space
the contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to lead in space exploration

look.title: First Words on the Moon
look.text: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
look.cite: Astronaut Neil Armstrong, NASA radio broadcast from the Moon, July 20, 1969
look.prompt: Why might Armstrong have called one step a giant leap for all people, not just for Americans?

check.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
check.why: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon first on July 20, 1969.

check.q: The Moon landing was a victory in a contest with which country?
check.why: The United States and the Soviet Union were rivals in the space race during the Cold War.

check.q: What does the story of Katherine Johnson show about the Moon landing?
choices: Only astronauts mattered to the mission
Many people worked behind the scenes to make it possible
check.why: Johnson was one of thousands of workers whose calculations and work made the flights possible.

lessons.title: Talking With Rivals
lessons.mainIdea: Nixon eased Cold War tensions through détente, a surprise visit to China and arms talks, and he ended the military draft.
reading: Nixon was known as a strong anti-Communist. Yet he surprised the world. With his adviser Henry Kissinger, he followed a plan called *détente*. Détente means an easing of tension between rivals. Nixon believed talking with Communist powers could make the world safer.

In February 1972, Nixon visited the People's Republic of China. No U.S. president had gone there since the Communists took power in 1949. He met the Chinese leader Mao Zedong and toured the Great Wall. Soon after, Nixon went to Moscow. He and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed an arms treaty called SALT I. It limited some nuclear weapons.

Nixon also slowly pulled U.S. troops out of Vietnam. The last American combat troops left in 1973. That same year, the *draft* ended. Before, young men could be ordered into the military. Now the country moved to an all-volunteer army. The draft had been a big cause of anger during the Vietnam War.

words.d: an easing of tension between rival countries
a system that requires people to serve in the military
a formal agreement between countries

look.title: An Unexpected Trip
look.text: Nixon had spent years warning about the dangers of communism. Then he became the first president to visit Communist China. Some of his supporters were shocked. Others said only a well-known anti-Communist could make such a trip without being called weak.
look.prompt: Why might a leader known for being tough be able to make peace moves that others could not?

check.q: What does the word détente mean?
choices: An easing of tension between rivals
check.why: Détente was Nixon's policy of lowering Cold War tensions through talks.

check.q: What happened in 1972?
choices: The United States entered World War II
check.why: Nixon's trip to the People's Republic of China took place in February 1972.

check.q: Why was ending the draft important to many Americans?
choices: The army wanted fewer soldiers than ever
It was part of the Moon landing
The draft had caused anger during the Vietnam War
check.why: Many young people protested being drafted to fight in Vietnam, so ending it answered a major complaint.

lessons.title: Protecting the Environment
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1970s, public concern about pollution led to Earth Day, the EPA and major laws to clean the air and water.
reading: By the late 1960s, pollution was easy to see. Smog hung over cities. Factories dumped waste into rivers and lakes. In 1969, the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland, Ohio, caught fire because it was so full of oil and trash. Many Americans decided something had to change.

On April 22, 1970, about 20 million Americans joined the first *Earth Day*. Senator Gaylord Nelson of Wisconsin helped start it. Students held teach-ins. People cleaned parks and marched in streets. The event showed that protecting the *environment* had wide support from both political parties.

Congress and President Nixon acted. In 1970, the government created the Environmental Protection Agency, or EPA. The Clean Air Act of 1970 set limits on air pollution. The Clean Water Act of 1972 worked to clean up rivers and lakes. The Endangered Species Act of 1973 protected animals and plants at risk of dying out, such as the bald eagle. Over time, the air and water in many places became much cleaner.

words.d: the air, water, land, plants and animals around us
a yearly day, first held in 1970, to show support for protecting the environment
harmful things, like smoke or waste, that make air, water or land dirty

look.title: A River on Fire
look.text: Imagine reading that a river in your state caught fire. It was not the first time. Oil and chemicals floating on the water had burned before. In 1969, news stories about the Cuyahoga River fire helped many Americans see pollution as a national problem, not just a local one.
look.prompt: Why can one shocking event push people and lawmakers to act on a problem that has existed for years?

check.q: Which agency was created in 1970 to protect the environment?
check.why: The Environmental Protection Agency was created in 1970.

check.q: What was the goal of the Clean Air Act of 1970?
choices: To send astronauts to the Moon
check.why: The Clean Air Act set limits on pollution in the air.

check.q: What does the first Earth Day show about Americans in 1970?
choices: Many people from both parties wanted to protect the environment
It was a protest against the Moon landing
check.why: About 20 million people took part, and support came from both parties.

lessons.title: The Watergate Scandal
lessons.mainIdea: Watergate began as a break-in and grew into a cover-up that led Richard Nixon to resign in 1974, the only president ever to do so.
reading: In June 1972, police arrested five men inside the Democratic Party's offices at the Watergate building in Washington, D.C. The burglars had ties to Nixon's reelection campaign. Nixon won the 1972 election in a landslide. But reporters kept digging. Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein of the Washington Post wrote story after story about the break-in.

The real trouble was the *cover-up*. People in the White House tried to hide what had happened and paid money to keep the burglars quiet. A Senate committee held hearings on TV. Then Americans learned that Nixon secretly taped talks in his office. Nixon refused to hand over the tapes. In July 1974, the Supreme Court ruled that he had to.

The tapes showed that Nixon had helped plan the cover-up soon after the break-in. A House committee had already voted to *impeach* him. Nixon knew he would likely be removed from office. On August 9, 1974, he resigned. Watergate showed that no one, not even a president, is above the law. It also left many Americans less trusting of their leaders.

words.d: an effort to hide a crime or wrongdoing
to formally charge a government official with serious wrongdoing
to give up a job or office by choice
an event where people in power are caught doing something wrong

look.title: Nixon Says Goodbye
look.text: I have never been a quitter. To leave office before my term is completed is abhorrent to every instinct in my body. But as President, I must put the interest of America first.
look.cite: President Richard Nixon, address to the nation announcing his resignation, August 8, 1974
look.prompt: What reason does Nixon give for resigning? What reason does he leave out?

check.q: What was the most serious problem in the Watergate scandal?
check.why: Hiding the crime, including by the president, turned a break-in into a national crisis.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in July 1974?
choices: Nixon could serve a third term
The Washington Post had to stop writing
Nixon had to turn over his tapes
check.why: The Court ruled that the president had to hand over the secret recordings.

check.q: What lesson about government did many people take from Watergate?
choices: No one is above the law, even a president
Congress has no power over presidents
check.why: The courts, Congress and the press all checked the president's power.

lessons.title: Ford and Hard Times
lessons.mainIdea: Gerald Ford took over a shaken nation facing an energy crisis, rising prices and slow growth.
reading: Gerald Ford had been a congressman from Michigan. He became vice president in 1973 and president in 1974. He was the only president never elected as president or vice president. Ford promised honesty. But a month later he *pardoned* Nixon, so Nixon could not be tried for any Watergate crimes. Ford said the nation needed to heal. Many Americans were angry.

Ford also faced money troubles. In 1973, Arab oil-producing nations stopped selling oil to the United States. They were angry about U.S. support for Israel in a war. Gas prices jumped. Drivers waited in long lines at gas stations. This *energy crisis* showed how much the country depended on oil from other places.

Prices for many goods kept rising. This is called *inflation*. At the same time, many people lost jobs. In the Midwest, some factories and steel mills began to close or cut workers. Americans started to call the region the Rust Belt. For many families, the 1970s were a time of worry about money.

words.d: to officially forgive a crime so a person cannot be punished for it
a time when fuel, such as oil or gas, is scarce and costly
a rise in prices over time, so money buys less

look.title: How Fast Prices Rose
look.unit: percent rise in prices that year
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index, rounded
look.prompt: In which year did prices rise fastest? What happened to inflation by 1983?

check.q: What did President Ford do that angered many Americans in 1974?
check.why: Ford's pardon meant Nixon could not be tried for Watergate crimes.

check.q: What caused long lines at gas stations in 1973?
choices: A new gas tax on bicycles
Arab oil producers stopped selling oil to the United States
check.why: The oil embargo cut supplies and raised prices quickly.

check.q: What is inflation?
choices: A rise in prices over time
A fall in prices over time
A drop in the number of workers
check.why: Inflation means prices go up, so the same money buys less.

lessons.title: Carter: Peace and a Hostage Crisis
lessons.mainIdea: Jimmy Carter helped make peace between Egypt and Israel but struggled with inflation and the Iran hostage crisis.
reading: In 1976, Jimmy Carter, a Democrat and former governor of Georgia, won the presidency. He was a peanut farmer and a Navy veteran. He promised to be honest with the American people. Carter made *human rights* a big part of his foreign policy. He spoke out against governments that jailed or hurt their own people.

Carter's greatest success came in 1978. He invited Egypt's president, Anwar Sadat, and Israel's prime minister, Menachem Begin, to Camp David in Maryland. The two countries had fought several wars. After 13 days of hard talks, they agreed on a plan for peace. The *Camp David Accords* led to a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel in 1979.

But troubles grew. Prices kept rising fast. In November 1979, students in Iran took over the U.S. embassy in Tehran. They held 52 Americans as *hostages*. A rescue attempt failed in 1980. The hostages were held for 444 days. They were freed on January 20, 1981, the day Carter left office.

words.d: basic freedoms and protections that belong to every person
a person held prisoner until demands are met
the 1978 agreements that led to peace between Egypt and Israel

look.title: A Crisis of Confidence
look.text: In a 1979 speech, Carter said the country faced a problem deeper than gas lines. He said many Americans were losing faith in the future and in their government. He asked people to work together and use less energy.
look.cite: President Jimmy Carter, address to the nation on energy, July 15, 1979 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might some listeners have liked this honest message, while others found it gloomy?

check.q: Which two countries made peace through the Camp David Accords?
check.why: Carter brought Sadat of Egypt and Begin of Israel together in 1978.

check.q: How long were the American hostages held in Iran?
check.why: The 52 hostages were held for 444 days and freed in January 1981.

check.q: Why did the hostage crisis hurt Carter politically?
choices: It made the government look unable to solve the problem
It happened after he left office
check.why: The long crisis and failed rescue made many voters feel the country was weak.

lessons.title: A New Direction in 1980
lessons.mainIdea: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election by promising smaller government, lower taxes and a stronger military.
reading: Ronald Reagan grew up in small towns in Illinois, including Dixon. He went to Eureka College in Illinois. He became a radio announcer and then a movie actor. Later he served two terms as governor of California. Reagan was a skilled speaker. People called him the Great Communicator.

In 1980, Reagan ran against Carter. He asked voters if they were better off than four years before. Many said no. Reagan won in a landslide. He was part of a growing *conservative* movement. Conservatives wanted a smaller federal government, lower taxes and fewer rules on business. Many also stressed religion and traditional family values.

Reagan's win changed American politics. Some voters who used to support Democrats, including many factory workers, now voted for him. People called them Reagan Democrats. Reagan was nearly killed by a gunman in March 1981 but recovered. That same year, he named Sandra Day O'Connor as the first woman on the Supreme Court.

words.d: a person who wants to keep traditions and usually prefers a smaller government role
an election won by a very large margin
a person who usually supports a larger government role in solving social problems

look.title: Reagan's View of Government
look.text: In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.
look.cite: President Ronald Reagan, First Inaugural Address, January 20, 1981
look.prompt: Reagan said this during a time of high inflation. What do you think he wanted to change? Why might others disagree?

check.q: Which state did Ronald Reagan grow up in?
check.why: Reagan grew up in small Illinois towns such as Dixon and went to Eureka College.

check.q: What did conservatives in 1980 generally want?
check.why: The conservative movement wanted to shrink the federal government's role and cut taxes.

check.q: Who was the first woman to serve on the Supreme Court?
check.why: Reagan named Sandra Day O'Connor in 1981.

lessons.title: Tax Cuts and Debates
lessons.mainIdea: Reagan cut taxes and business rules and built up the military, and Americans still debate the results.
reading: In 1981, Congress passed large *tax cuts* that Reagan asked for. Reagan believed lower taxes would let people and businesses keep more money. He said they would spend and invest it, and the economy would grow. Supporters called this supply-side economics. Reagan also pushed *deregulation*, or cutting government rules on business. Carter had already begun this with airlines and trucking.

At first, the economy got worse. In 1982, many people were out of work. The Federal Reserve had raised interest rates very high to stop inflation. It worked. Inflation fell sharply. By 1983, the economy was growing again, and it kept growing for years.

Reagan also spent much more on the military. With lower taxes and higher spending, the government borrowed a lot. The national *debt* nearly tripled while Reagan was president. Supporters said his policies beat inflation, created jobs and helped win the Cold War. Critics said the tax cuts helped the rich most, cut programs for poor people, and left huge debts. Americans still argue about this.

words.d: a law that lowers the amount of tax people or businesses pay
removing or reducing government rules on businesses
money that is owed; the national debt is what the government has borrowed

look.title: Two Views of the 1980s
look.text: A supporter says: Lower taxes rewarded hard work, the economy grew for years, and inflation finally came down. A critic says: The gap between rich and poor grew, many factory workers lost jobs, and the government piled up debt that future generations must pay.
look.prompt: What evidence from the lesson could each person use? What more information would help you decide?

check.q: What is deregulation?
check.why: Deregulation means removing or reducing rules that government places on businesses.

check.q: What happened to the national debt under Reagan?
check.why: Lower taxes plus higher military spending led the government to borrow much more.

check.q: Why did Reagan believe tax cuts would help the economy?
choices: The government would hire more workers
People and businesses would spend and invest the extra money
check.why: Supply-side ideas said money left in private hands would fuel growth.

lessons.title: A Changing Population
lessons.mainIdea: New immigration, movement to the Sun Belt and new leaders changed who Americans were and where they lived.
reading: A 1965 law ended old limits that favored immigrants from Europe. After that, more immigrants came from Latin America and Asia. After the Vietnam War ended in 1975, many refugees came from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. The Refugee Act of 1980 set up a system for welcoming people fleeing danger. In 1986, a new law gave legal status to about 2.7 million immigrants who had come without permission.

Americans were also on the move. Many left the Northeast and Midwest for the *Sun Belt*, the warm states of the South and Southwest. Jobs, cheaper housing and air conditioning drew them. States like Texas, Florida and Arizona grew fast. They gained seats in Congress.

New voices rose in politics. In 1983, Chicago voters elected Harold Washington as the city's first Black mayor. In 1984, Geraldine Ferraro became the first woman chosen by a major party to run for vice president. Latino and Asian American leaders won more offices too. The nation was becoming more *diverse*.

words.d: the warm states of the South and Southwest
made up of many different kinds of people
a person who flees their home country to escape war or danger

look.title: Americans Born in Another Country
look.cite: U.S. Census Bureau, foreign-born population, rounded
look.prompt: About how much did the foreign-born population grow from 1970 to 1990? What lesson facts help explain it?

check.q: After 1965, more immigrants came from which regions?
check.why: The 1965 law ended limits that favored Europe, so more people came from Latin America and Asia.

check.q: Who became Chicago's first Black mayor in 1983?
check.why: Chicago voters elected Harold Washington in 1983.

check.q: Why did states like Texas and Florida gain seats in Congress?
choices: Congress added seats only for the South
People left them for the Midwest
Their populations grew as people moved to the Sun Belt
check.why: Seats in the House are based on population, and Sun Belt states grew fast.

lessons.title: Reagan and Gorbachev
lessons.mainIdea: After a tense arms buildup, Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev built trust and signed a treaty to destroy some nuclear weapons.
reading: In his first years, Reagan took a hard line against the Soviet Union. He built up the military and called the Soviet Union an evil empire. He also proposed a system to shoot down nuclear missiles from space. Critics called it Star Wars. Many people feared the arms race could lead to nuclear war.

In 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev became the Soviet leader. He was younger than earlier leaders and wanted change. The Soviet economy was failing. Gorbachev allowed more open talk, called *glasnost*. He also tried to reform the economy, called *perestroika*.

Reagan and Gorbachev met several times. At first they could not agree. But they came to trust each other. In 1987, they signed the INF Treaty. For the first time, the two sides agreed to destroy a whole type of nuclear missile. Reagan said the U.S. would trust but verify, which meant checking that the Soviets kept their word.

words.d: Gorbachev's policy of more openness and free speech in the Soviet Union
Gorbachev's plan to reform the Soviet economy
a contest between countries to build more and stronger weapons

look.title: A Challenge in Berlin
look.text: General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
look.cite: President Ronald Reagan, speech at the Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin, June 12, 1987
look.prompt: Reagan spoke next to the Berlin Wall. Why do you think he used the wall as a symbol?

check.q: What was glasnost?
choices: A Soviet policy of more openness
check.why: Glasnost allowed more open talk and criticism in the Soviet Union.

check.q: What did the INF Treaty of 1987 do?
choices: It destroyed a whole type of nuclear missile
check.why: The INF Treaty was the first to get rid of an entire kind of nuclear weapon.

check.q: Why was Gorbachev willing to make changes?
choices: The Soviet Union had won the arms race
He wanted to build a new wall
Reagan forced him out of office
check.why: Serious economic problems pushed Gorbachev to try reform and reduce military costs.

lessons.title: Walls Come Down
lessons.mainIdea: In 1989, Communist governments in Eastern Europe fell, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself broke apart, ending the Cold War.
reading: In 1989, change spread across Eastern Europe. In Poland, a workers' movement called *Solidarity*, led by Lech Wałęsa, won free elections. Hungary opened its border to Austria. Huge peaceful protests filled the streets of East Germany and Czechoslovakia. Gorbachev did not send troops to stop them.

On November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall opened. By the end of the year, Communist governments had fallen in most of Eastern Europe. In October 1990, East and West Germany *reunified*, or became one country again. President George H.W. Bush worked with other leaders to make these changes peaceful.

Inside the Soviet Union, the republics that made it up wanted to be free. In December 1991, the Soviet Union broke apart into 15 independent countries, including Russia and Ukraine. Gorbachev resigned. The Cold War, which had lasted more than 40 years, was over. The United States was now the world's only *superpower*.

words.d: to join parts of something back together into one
a nation with enormous military and economic power
a Polish workers' movement that helped end Communist rule in Poland

look.title: What Ended the Cold War?
look.text: People give different reasons for the end of the Cold War. Some point to Reagan's military buildup and firm stand. Some credit Gorbachev's reforms and his choice not to use force. Others point to ordinary people in Poland, East Germany and elsewhere who marched and demanded freedom.
look.prompt: Which reason do you think mattered most? Could more than one be true at once?

check.q: When did the Soviet Union break apart?
check.why: The Soviet Union dissolved into 15 countries in December 1991.

check.q: What happened to Germany in October 1990?
choices: It was split into four parts
check.why: The two Germanys became one country again less than a year after the wall opened.

check.q: Why was Gorbachev's choice not to send troops important in 1989?
choices: It kept the Berlin Wall closed
It let peaceful protests topple Communist governments
It made Eastern Europe join the Soviet Union
check.why: Without Soviet force behind them, the Communist governments could not hold on to power.

lessons.title: New Rights and a New War
lessons.mainIdea: In 1990 the Americans with Disabilities Act protected millions of people, and in 1991 the U.S. led a coalition to push Iraq out of Kuwait.
reading: For years, people with disabilities faced closed doors. Many buildings had only stairs. Many buses had no lifts. Employers could refuse to hire someone because of a disability. Activists fought back. In March 1990, dozens left their wheelchairs and crawled up the steps of the U.S. Capitol to demand a law.

In July 1990, President George H.W. Bush signed the *Americans with Disabilities Act*, or ADA. It banned *discrimination* against people with disabilities in jobs, schools, stores and transportation. It required ramps, accessible buses and other changes. Today, curb cuts, elevators and captioned videos are common partly because of the ADA.

Meanwhile, trouble came in the Middle East. In August 1990, Iraq's leader, Saddam Hussein, invaded the small oil-rich country of Kuwait. President Bush built a *coalition* of more than 30 nations. In January 1991, the coalition attacked. The Persian Gulf War ended in about six weeks, and Kuwait was freed. Saddam Hussein, however, stayed in power in Iraq.

words.d: unfair treatment of people because of who they are
a group of nations or people working together for a shared goal
a 1990 law that protects people with disabilities from discrimination

look.title: Signing the ADA
look.text: Let the shameful wall of exclusion finally come tumbling down.
look.cite: President George H.W. Bush, remarks at the signing of the Americans with Disabilities Act, July 26, 1990
look.prompt: Bush spoke less than a year after the Berlin Wall opened. Why might he have chosen the image of a wall?

check.q: What does the ADA do?
choices: Bans discrimination against people with disabilities
check.why: The Americans with Disabilities Act protects people with disabilities in jobs, schools and public places.

check.q: What started the Persian Gulf War?
check.why: Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait in 1990 led to the U.S.-led coalition attack in 1991.

check.q: Why did activists crawl up the Capitol steps in 1990?
choices: To show how barriers kept people with disabilities out
To celebrate the end of the Cold War
check.why: The crawl made the problem of inaccessible buildings impossible for lawmakers to ignore.

choices: The fall of the Berlin Wall
review.why: The Moon landing was in 1969; the others came in 1974, 1978 and 1989.

choices: He wanted to become a senator
The Watergate tapes showed he helped cover up the break-in
review.why: The tapes proved his role in the cover-up, and he faced likely removal by Congress.

review.q: Which problem troubled both Ford and Carter?
review.why: Inflation and oil shortages hurt the economy through much of the 1970s.

choices: An easing of Cold War tensions
review.why: Nixon used détente to talk with the Soviet Union and China.

review.q: What did the 1970 Clean Air Act and 1972 Clean Water Act have in common?
choices: Both dealt with the space race
review.why: Both laws set limits on pollution to protect the environment.

review.q: How did Reagan's ideas about government differ from those behind the Great Society?
choices: Reagan wanted a smaller federal government
Reagan wanted many new federal programs
review.why: Reagan and conservatives believed government had grown too large and wanted to cut taxes and rules.

review.q: Which leaders signed the INF Treaty in 1987?
review.why: Reagan and Gorbachev agreed to destroy a whole class of nuclear missiles.

review.q: Which event marked the end of the Cold War?
choices: The breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991
review.why: When the Soviet Union broke apart, the rival superpower no longer existed.

chapters.title: Bridge to the 21st Century
chapters.bigQuestion: How have technology, conflict and a changing population shaped the United States since 1990?

story.title: New Americans Take the Oath
story.kicker: Every year, hundreds of thousands of people raise their right hands and become U.S. citizens.
paragraphs: Picture a courtroom in downtown Chicago on a weekday morning. Rows of chairs are full. Families squeeze in along the walls, holding small American flags. The people in the front rows were born in dozens of countries. Some came from Mexico, India or the Philippines. Others came from Poland, Nigeria or Iraq. Today, they will become citizens of the United States.

Some of them first arrived as refugees. A refugee is a person forced to flee home because of war or danger, and who cannot safely go back. Before coming, refugees go through long interviews and security checks. The wait can take years. When they land, local groups often help them find an apartment, enroll children in school and look for work. In the Chicago area, several such groups have helped families from places like Syria, Afghanistan, Congo and Burma.

Becoming a citizen is a long road. Most people must first be lawful permanent residents, often called green card holders, usually for five years. Then they fill out an application, get fingerprinted and have an interview. They must show they can read, write and speak basic English. They also take a civics test with questions like: What is the supreme law of the land? Who was the first president?

Now, at the ceremony, a judge or official asks everyone to stand. Together, they read the Oath of Allegiance. They promise to support and defend the Constitution. When they finish, they are Americans. People cheer. Children wave flags. Some new citizens cry. Many stop at a table on the way out to register to vote.

Scenes like this take place across the country all year long. They are one small part of a bigger story. Since 1990, the United States has changed fast. New technology connected the world. The nation faced terrible attacks, wars, storms, a deep recession and a pandemic. Through it all, people kept arriving, and the country kept debating what it means to be American.
story.think: What might a new citizen feel on the day they take the oath? Why do you think many register to vote right away?

lessons.title: After the Cold War
lessons.mainIdea: With the Cold War over, Americans turned their attention to problems at home and elected Bill Clinton in 1992.
reading: George H.W. Bush was president when the Cold War ended. His popularity soared after the Persian Gulf War in 1991. But then the economy slowed down. Many people lost jobs. Bush had promised not to raise taxes, but he agreed to a budget deal that did. Some voters felt he had broken his word.

In 1992, Bill Clinton, the Democratic governor of Arkansas, ran against Bush. A businessman named Ross Perot also ran as an *independent* candidate. Perot won almost one-fifth of the popular vote, a strong result for a third candidate. Clinton won the election. Clinton called himself a New Democrat, a *moderate* who wanted to mix ideas from both parties.

With the Soviet Union gone, the United States faced a new kind of world. There was no single rival superpower. But conflicts still broke out. In the 1990s, U.S. troops took part in peacekeeping missions, such as in Bosnia and Kosovo in southeastern Europe. Americans debated how much the country should get involved in faraway conflicts.

words.d: a candidate or voter who does not belong to a political party
a person whose political views are in the middle, not far to either side
sending troops to help keep peace between groups that have been fighting

look.title: A Hopeful Beginning
look.text: There is nothing wrong with America that cannot be cured by what is right with America.
look.cite: President Bill Clinton, First Inaugural Address, January 20, 1993
look.prompt: What do you think Clinton meant? What might he count as right with America?

check.q: Who won the presidential election of 1992?
check.why: Clinton, the governor of Arkansas, defeated Bush and Perot.

check.q: Why did Bush lose support after the Gulf War?
choices: The economy slowed and he agreed to raise taxes
check.why: A weak economy and a broken tax promise hurt him with voters.

check.q: What made the world different for the U.S. after 1991?
choices: The U.S. left the United Nations
check.why: With the Soviet Union gone, the U.S. was the only superpower, though conflicts continued.

lessons.title: Trade and a Budget Surplus
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1990s, the U.S. signed NAFTA, the economy boomed and the federal government balanced its budget for the first time in decades.
reading: In 1993, Congress approved the North American Free Trade Agreement, or *NAFTA*. It took effect in 1994. NAFTA removed most taxes on trade among the United States, Canada and Mexico. Supporters said it would lower prices and help businesses sell more. Critics, including many labor unions, said factories would move to Mexico, where wages were lower. Both sides pointed to evidence in later years.

The economy grew for most of the 1990s. Unemployment fell. New technology companies created many jobs. Tax money poured into the government. Clinton and a Republican-led Congress also agreed on spending limits and welfare changes. By 1998, the government had a budget *surplus*. It took in more money than it spent for the first time since 1969.

Clinton's presidency also had a scandal. He was accused of lying under oath about a relationship with a young White House worker. In 1998, the House of Representatives *impeached* him on charges of perjury, or lying under oath, and obstruction of justice. In 1999, the Senate held a trial and did not remove him. Clinton became the second president to be impeached, after Andrew Johnson.

words.d: the North American Free Trade Agreement among the U.S., Canada and Mexico
an amount left over; a budget surplus means more money comes in than goes out
to formally charge a government official with serious wrongdoing

look.title: Two Sides of Free Trade
look.text: A family in Illinois buys cheaper clothes and electronics made in other countries. A farmer sells more corn and soybeans to Mexico. But down the road, a factory closes and moves some of its work to Mexico, and hundreds of workers lose their jobs.
look.prompt: Who gains and who loses from free trade in this example? How might a leader try to help those who lose?

check.q: Which three countries were part of NAFTA?
choices: The United States, China and Japan
The United States, Canada and Mexico
The United States, Britain and France
check.why: NAFTA covered trade across North America.

check.q: What does a budget surplus mean?
choices: The government spends more than it takes in
The government takes in more money than it spends
check.why: A surplus is money left over after spending.

check.q: Why did many labor unions oppose NAFTA?
choices: They feared factory jobs would move to Mexico
They wanted to end trade with Canada
check.why: Lower wages in Mexico could lead companies to move work there.

lessons.title: The Digital Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: Personal computers and the internet changed how Americans work, learn, shop and talk to each other.
reading: In the 1970s, computers were huge machines used mostly by governments, colleges and big companies. Then small *personal computers* came along. Apple sold its first computers in the late 1970s. IBM released its personal computer in 1981. Microsoft's software ran on millions of machines. By the 1990s, many homes and schools had a computer.

The *internet* began as a U.S. government project that linked computers at research centers. In 1989, British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web, a way to link pages of information. In 1993, students and staff at the University of Illinois in Urbana-Champaign released Mosaic. It was one of the first easy-to-use web *browsers*, and it helped millions of people go online.

New companies grew quickly. Amazon started selling books online in 1995. Google began in 1998. People sent email instead of letters. Many jobs now needed computer skills. This *digital* economy made some people rich. But not everyone had equal access. People called this gap the digital divide.

words.d: a computer small and cheap enough for one person to use at home or work
a worldwide network that connects computers
a program used to find and view pages on the World Wide Web
using computer technology and electronic data

look.title: The Digital Divide
look.text: In the late 1990s, a student in a wealthy suburb might have a fast computer at home. A student in a poor rural area or city neighborhood might only use one at a library, if at all. As more homework, jobs and news moved online, the gap began to matter more.
look.prompt: How could the digital divide affect a student's future? What could communities or schools do about it?

check.q: Where was the Mosaic web browser created?
check.why: Mosaic was released in 1993 at the University of Illinois in Urbana-Champaign.

check.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
check.why: Tim Berners-Lee created the Web in 1989.

check.q: What is the digital divide?
choices: The gap between people who have access to technology and those who do not
A split in the Democratic Party
check.why: The digital divide describes unequal access to computers and the internet.

lessons.title: A Close Election in 2000
lessons.mainIdea: The 2000 presidential election was so close in Florida that the Supreme Court's decision in Bush v. Gore settled the outcome.
reading: In 2000, Vice President Al Gore, a Democrat, ran against Texas governor George W. Bush, a Republican. Bush was the son of the former president. On election night, the result came down to Florida. Whoever won Florida's *electoral votes* would win the presidency. The count there was extremely close.

Florida began a *recount*. Some ballots were hard to read, and the rules for counting them were unclear. Lawyers for both sides went to court. For weeks, the country did not know who its next president would be. The Florida Supreme Court ordered more hand counts.

On December 12, 2000, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 in *Bush v. Gore*. The decision stopped the recount. Bush was declared the winner of Florida by 537 votes. That gave him the presidency, even though Gore won more votes nationwide. Supporters of the ruling said it ended a chaotic process that treated ballots unequally. Critics said every vote should have been counted. Gore accepted the result.

words.d: a vote cast by a state's electors; a candidate needs a majority of them to become president
counting votes again to check the result
the 2000 Supreme Court case that stopped the Florida recount

look.title: Winning Without the Most Votes
look.text: In 2000, Gore won about half a million more votes across the country, but Bush won more electoral votes. This had happened a few times before, in the 1800s. Some people say the Electoral College protects smaller states. Others say the candidate with the most votes should win.
look.prompt: What are the arguments for and against the Electoral College? Which do you find stronger, and why?

check.q: Which state decided the 2000 election?
check.why: The winner of Florida's electoral votes would win, and the count there was extremely close.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court do in Bush v. Gore?
check.why: The 5 to 4 ruling ended the recount, leaving Bush the winner.

check.q: Why was the 2000 election unusual?
choices: The winner received fewer votes nationwide than the loser
check.why: Gore won the national popular vote, but Bush won the Electoral College.

lessons.title: September 11, 2001
lessons.mainIdea: On September 11, 2001, terrorists attacked the United States, killing nearly 3,000 people and changing the nation's sense of safety.
reading: On the morning of September 11, 2001, 19 men from a terrorist group called *al Qaeda* took over four passenger airplanes. They crashed two into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. Both towers fell. They crashed a third plane into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the U.S. military, near Washington, D.C.

On the fourth plane, United Flight 93, passengers learned what had happened by phone. They fought back against the hijackers. The plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Everyone on board died, but the plane did not reach its target in Washington. Nearly 3,000 people were killed that day, including hundreds of firefighters and police officers.

Al Qaeda was led by Osama bin Laden. The group practiced *terrorism*, using violence against ordinary people to create fear for political goals. Americans were shocked and grieving. Many gave blood, raised money and flew flags. Muslim Americans, and people mistaken for Muslims, sometimes faced hate and violence. Leaders reminded the nation that the attackers did not represent a whole religion.

words.d: the use of violence against ordinary people to create fear and reach political goals
the terrorist group, led by Osama bin Laden, that carried out the September 11 attacks
a person who takes control of a vehicle, such as a plane, by force

look.title: The President Speaks That Night
look.text: Terrorist attacks can shake the foundations of our biggest buildings, but they cannot touch the foundation of America. These acts shatter steel, but they cannot dent the steel of American resolve.
look.cite: President George W. Bush, address to the nation, September 11, 2001
look.prompt: What two meanings of foundation and steel does Bush use? What message was he sending?

check.q: Which group carried out the September 11 attacks?
check.why: Al Qaeda, led by Osama bin Laden, planned and carried out the attacks.

check.q: What happened on United Flight 93?
choices: Passengers fought back and the plane crashed in Pennsylvania
It hit the World Trade Center
check.why: Passengers fought the hijackers, and the plane crashed near Shanksville before reaching Washington.

check.q: Why did some leaders remind Americans that the attackers did not represent all Muslims?
choices: Some Muslim Americans faced hate and violence after the attacks
check.why: Innocent people were being blamed and targeted because of their religion or appearance.

lessons.title: Security and Two Wars
lessons.mainIdea: After 9/11, the U.S. created new security agencies and fought long wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
reading: The government moved fast to protect the country. Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act in 2001. It gave the government more power to watch and investigate suspected terrorists. In 2002, Congress created the *Department of Homeland Security* to guard borders, airports and other targets. Airport security became much stricter. Some Americans worried that the new powers went too far and threatened privacy.

In October 2001, the United States and its allies attacked Afghanistan. Its rulers, the *Taliban*, had sheltered al Qaeda. The Taliban quickly lost power, but fighting went on for years. In May 2011, U.S. forces found and killed Osama bin Laden in Pakistan. The last U.S. troops left Afghanistan in August 2021, and the Taliban took control again.

In March 2003, the U.S. led an invasion of Iraq and overthrew Saddam Hussein. Bush said Iraq had dangerous weapons of mass destruction. No such weapons were found. A long and costly *insurgency*, or armed uprising, followed. Americans were deeply divided about the Iraq War. Most U.S. troops left Iraq in 2011. Thousands of U.S. troops and many more Iraqis died in the war.

words.d: a federal department created in 2002 to protect the country from attacks and disasters
the group that ruled Afghanistan and sheltered al Qaeda
an armed uprising against a government or occupying force

look.title: A New Kind of War
look.text: Our war on terror begins with al Qaeda, but it does not end there. It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped and defeated.
look.cite: President George W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, September 20, 2001
look.prompt: How was this war different from earlier wars against a single country? What challenges might that create?

check.q: Why did the U.S. attack Afghanistan in 2001?
choices: Its Taliban rulers sheltered al Qaeda
check.why: The Taliban had given al Qaeda a safe place to plan attacks.

check.q: What reason did President Bush give for the 2003 invasion of Iraq?
choices: Iraq had weapons of mass destruction
check.why: Bush said Iraq had dangerous weapons, but none were found.

check.q: Why did some Americans criticize the PATRIOT Act?
choices: They thought it cut taxes too much
check.why: Critics said the new surveillance powers could reach too far into people's private lives.

lessons.title: Hurricane Katrina
lessons.mainIdea: In 2005, Hurricane Katrina flooded New Orleans, and the slow response raised hard questions about government and fairness.
reading: In late August 2005, Hurricane Katrina slammed into the Gulf Coast of Louisiana and Mississippi. In New Orleans, the storm caused *levees* to fail. Levees are walls built to hold back water. About 80 percent of the city flooded. Some neighborhoods were under many feet of water.

Many people had left before the storm. But thousands could not, often because they had no car or money to travel. Many of them were poor, elderly or Black. People waited on rooftops for rescue. Thousands crowded into the Superdome and the convention center with little food, water or medical care. More than 1,800 people died because of the storm.

Help from local, state and federal governments was slow and poorly organized. The head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, or *FEMA*, resigned. Many Americans asked why the richest nation in the world could not do better. Volunteers came from across the country. Many New Orleans residents moved away for good, and rebuilding took years.

words.d: a wall or bank built to keep a river or lake from flooding
the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which helps during disasters
to leave a dangerous place to get to safety

look.title: Who Could Leave?
look.text: Officials told people in New Orleans to evacuate before Katrina hit. For a family with a car, gas money and relatives in another city, leaving was hard but possible. For an elderly person living alone without a car, or a family with no savings, leaving was much harder.
look.prompt: How did wealth and resources affect who was in danger during Katrina? What could make disaster plans fairer?

check.q: Why did most of New Orleans flood during Katrina?
check.why: When the levees failed, water poured into about 80 percent of the city.

check.q: Why were many people unable to evacuate?
choices: They were not told about the storm
The roads were closed for years
They had no car or money to travel
They were all out of the country
check.why: Many poor and elderly residents lacked the resources to leave.

check.q: What was a major criticism after Katrina?
choices: The storm was predicted wrong by a year
Government help was slow and poorly organized
check.why: The slow response at every level of government was widely criticized.

lessons.title: The Great Recession
lessons.mainIdea: In 2008, a housing crash and a banking crisis caused the worst economic downturn since the Great Depression.
reading: In the early 2000s, home prices rose fast. Banks made many risky *mortgages*, or home loans, to people who might not be able to pay them back. Banks then bundled and sold these loans as investments. When home prices began to fall around 2006 and 2007, many people could not pay. They lost their homes.

The losses spread through the banking system. In September 2008, a huge investment bank, Lehman Brothers, collapsed. Panic hit Wall Street. Congress passed a plan to spend up to 700 billion dollars to rescue banks. Some people called it a *bailout*. Supporters said it kept the economy from collapsing. Critics said it rewarded the banks that caused the problem.

The *Great Recession* lasted from late 2007 to mid-2009. Millions of Americans lost jobs. Many families lost savings and homes. In 2009, Congress passed a large spending plan to boost the economy. The auto industry got government loans. Recovery was slow. It took years for jobs to come back.

words.d: a loan used to buy a house
government money given to rescue a failing business or bank
the deep economic downturn that lasted from late 2007 to mid-2009
a period when the economy shrinks and many people lose jobs

look.title: Jobs Lost in the Great Recession
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, annual average unemployment rate, rounded
look.prompt: When was unemployment highest? What does the data show about how fast jobs came back?

check.q: What helped start the Great Recession?
choices: Risky home loans and falling home prices
The fall of the Berlin Wall
A drought in the Dust Bowl
check.why: When home prices fell, many borrowers could not pay, and banks lost huge sums.

check.q: What is a mortgage?
choices: A loan used to buy a house
check.why: A mortgage is a home loan that is paid back over many years.

check.q: Why was the bank rescue plan controversial?
choices: It raised taxes on students only
Critics said it rewarded banks that caused the crisis
check.why: Supporters said it prevented collapse, but critics said banks should not be rescued for their own mistakes.

lessons.title: A Historic Election
lessons.mainIdea: In 2008, Barack Obama of Illinois became the first African American elected president, and his health care law sparked a long debate.
reading: Barack Obama was born in Hawaii in 1961. As a young man, he moved to Chicago and worked as a *community organizer* on the city's South Side. He later taught law and served in the Illinois state senate. In 2004, Illinois voters elected him to the U.S. Senate.

In 2008, Obama won the Democratic nomination after a close race with Hillary Clinton. He then defeated Republican John McCain. On election night, a huge crowd gathered in Chicago's Grant Park to hear him speak. Obama became the first African American president. Many Americans saw it as a milestone in a country shaped by slavery and segregation. He won reelection in 2012.

In 2010, Obama signed the *Affordable Care Act*, often called Obamacare. It aimed to help millions of uninsured people get health insurance. It stopped insurance companies from turning people away for health problems they already had. Supporters said it made health care fairer. Critics said it cost too much and gave the government too much power. In 2012, the Supreme Court upheld most of the law.

words.d: a person who helps neighbors work together to solve local problems
a 2010 law meant to help more Americans get health insurance
not having insurance to help pay for health care

look.title: Obama's First Inaugural
look.text: On this day, we gather because we have chosen hope over fear, unity of purpose over conflict and discord.
look.cite: President Barack Obama, First Inaugural Address, January 20, 2009
look.prompt: Obama took office during the Great Recession and two wars. Why might he have focused on hope and unity?

check.q: Which state did Barack Obama represent in the U.S. Senate?
check.why: Obama built his career in Chicago and was elected a U.S. senator from Illinois in 2004.

check.q: What was a main goal of the Affordable Care Act?
choices: To help more people get health insurance
check.why: The law aimed to reduce the number of uninsured Americans.

check.q: Why did many people see Obama's 2008 election as a milestone?
choices: He was the first African American president
He was the youngest person ever to vote
He was the first president from California
He was elected without any votes
check.why: In a nation shaped by slavery and segregation, electing a Black president was a historic first.

lessons.title: A Connected World
lessons.mainIdea: Smartphones, social media and global trade have tied Americans closely to one another and to the rest of the world.
reading: In 2007, Apple released the first iPhone. Soon, most Americans carried a *smartphone*, a small computer that fits in a pocket. People could look up facts, take photos, find directions and shop anywhere. Social media sites, such as Facebook, which began in 2004, let people share news and ideas instantly.

These tools changed daily life. Protest movements could organize quickly. Small businesses could reach customers everywhere. But there were problems too. False information could spread fast. Many people worried about privacy and about how much time young people spent online. Americans still debate how, or whether, to regulate tech companies.

*Globalization* also grew. This means the world's economies and cultures became more closely linked. A phone might be designed in California, built in Asia with parts from many countries, and sold everywhere. Global trade lowered many prices. It also cost some American factory jobs. China became a major trading partner and rival of the United States.

Scientists report that Earth's *climate* is warming, mostly because burning coal, oil and gas releases heat-trapping gases. In 2015, the U.S. helped create the Paris climate agreement to cut these gases. Since then, presidents of different parties have left it, rejoined it and moved to leave it again. Meanwhile, the country has become a top producer of oil and natural gas, and it also makes more electricity from wind and solar power each year.

words.d: a mobile phone that works like a small computer and connects to the internet
websites and apps where people share posts, photos and messages
the process of the world's economies and cultures becoming more connected
the usual weather patterns of a place over a long time

look.title: Energy Choices
look.text: A coal-mining town depends on jobs at the mine. A farm family worries about droughts and floods. A solar company wants to hire workers. A family on a tight budget worries about the cost of gas and electric bills. Each group has a stake in the country's energy choices.
look.prompt: What might a coal miner, a farmer, a solar panel installer and a young student each want leaders to consider about energy?

check.q: What is globalization?
choices: A new way to measure the Earth
The world's economies and cultures becoming more connected
check.why: Globalization means countries are more closely linked by trade, travel and communication.

check.q: When was the first iPhone released?
check.why: Apple released the first iPhone in 2007.

check.q: What is one concern about social media?
choices: It only works on computers from the 1970s
check.why: Because posts spread instantly, untrue claims can reach millions before they are checked.

lessons.title: Recent Elections and a Pandemic
lessons.mainIdea: Close, hard-fought elections and the COVID-19 pandemic marked the years after 2016.
reading: In 2016, Republican Donald Trump, a New York businessman, defeated Democrat Hillary Clinton. Clinton was the first woman nominated for president by a major party. Clinton won more votes nationwide, but Trump won the Electoral College. In 2020, Democrat Joe Biden defeated Trump. Kamala Harris became the first woman, and the first Black and South Asian American, to serve as vice president.

Trump did not accept the 2020 results and said the election was unfair. Courts and state officials rejected those claims. On January 6, 2021, while Congress was counting the electoral votes, a crowd of Trump supporters broke into the U.S. Capitol. Congress finished counting that night. In 2024, Trump defeated Harris. He became the second president, after Grover Cleveland, to serve two terms that were not back to back.

In early 2020, a new disease called COVID-19 spread around the world. It became a *pandemic*, a disease outbreak across many countries. Schools and businesses closed for months. Many people worked and learned from home. Scientists quickly developed *vaccines*, which became available in December 2020. By 2022, more than one million Americans had died of COVID-19. Americans disagreed about rules such as mask requirements and closings.

words.d: an outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries
a medicine that helps the body protect itself against a disease
the system of electors from each state that formally chooses the president

look.title: Hard Choices in a Pandemic
look.text: In 2020, leaders had to make fast choices with limited information. Closing schools and businesses might slow the spread of the virus. But closings also hurt learning, jobs and people's mental health. Different states and cities made different choices.
look.prompt: What should leaders weigh when a choice protects some people but harms others? Who should they listen to?

check.q: Who was the first woman to serve as vice president?
check.why: Kamala Harris became vice president in January 2021.

check.q: What is a pandemic?
choices: A disease outbreak across many countries
check.why: COVID-19 became a pandemic because it spread worldwide.

check.q: Why did many schools close in 2020?
choices: To slow the spread of COVID-19
check.why: Leaders closed schools to reduce contact and slow the virus.

lessons.title: A Diverse Nation Takes Part
lessons.mainIdea: Immigration keeps changing the country, and citizens shape its future by voting, serving and speaking up.
reading: Today, about one in seven people living in the United States was born in another country. The largest groups come from Mexico, India, China and the Philippines, among many others. The Chicago area is home to large Mexican American, Polish American and Indian American communities. The Latino and Asian American populations have grown fast.

*Immigration* is also a subject of strong debate. Millions of people live in the country without legal permission. Some Americans want stricter border security and more deportations. Others want a path to citizenship for people who have lived and worked here for years. Many want both. Congress has debated major immigration changes for decades without passing a full plan.

In a democracy, citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Adults who are citizens can vote and serve on juries. People of any age can volunteer, write to leaders, attend public meetings and learn about issues from reliable sources. Students can serve on school councils and help their communities. The story of the United States is still being written, and each person has a part in it.

words.d: moving to a new country to live there
a legal member of a country with rights and responsibilities
the legal process by which an immigrant becomes a citizen

look.title: The Oath of Allegiance
look.text: I hereby declare, on oath, that I absolutely and entirely renounce and abjure all allegiance and fidelity to any foreign prince, potentate, state, or sovereignty … that I will support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States of America against all enemies, foreign and domestic …
look.cite: Oath of Allegiance for new U.S. citizens, U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 8 CFR 337.1
look.prompt: In your own words, what two big promises do new citizens make in this oath?

check.why: Roughly 14 percent of U.S. residents were born abroad.

check.q: Which is a responsibility adult citizens can carry out?
check.why: Jury service is a duty of citizens in the U.S. justice system.

check.q: What is naturalization?
choices: The process by which an immigrant becomes a citizen
check.why: Naturalization includes an application, interview, tests and the oath.

review.why: NAFTA took effect in 1994; the others came in 2001, 2005 and 2007 to 2009.

review.q: What came with the strong economy of the late 1990s?
review.why: Economic growth and budget deals produced the first surplus since 1969.

review.q: Which invention from the University of Illinois helped people use the Web?
review.why: Mosaic, released in 1993, made the Web easy to use.

review.q: What was one result of the September 11 attacks?
choices: The Department of Homeland Security was created
review.why: Congress created the department in 2002 to protect the country.

review.q: Why did the United States go to war in Afghanistan?
choices: The Taliban sheltered al Qaeda after 9/11
review.why: The U.S. aimed to defeat al Qaeda and remove the Taliban that protected it.

review.q: How were Hurricane Katrina and the COVID-19 pandemic alike?
choices: Both raised hard questions about how government responds to emergencies
review.why: In both crises, Americans debated how well leaders prepared and responded.

review.q: What made the elections of 2000 and 2016 similar?
choices: The winner lost the national popular vote
Both were decided by the Supreme Court
No one ran against the winner
review.why: Bush in 2000 and Trump in 2016 won the Electoral College but not the popular vote.

review.q: Which statement about immigration today is accurate?
choices: All Americans agree on immigration laws
Americans disagree about border security and paths to citizenship
review.why: Immigration remains a major debate, with different views on security and legal status.
